question.text: Scenario: Mahesh (age 50) is a successful businessman with a net worth of Rs. 10 crore. Annual income: Rs. 60,00,000. Wife Neha (age 47). Two adult children: son Arjun (age 25, working in the family business) and daughter Priya (age 22, MBA student). Assets: residential house Rs. 3,00,00,000, business equity Rs. 4,00,00,000, equity mutual funds Rs. 1,50,00,000, FD and debt mutual funds Rs. 80,00,000, gold and real estate investments Rs. 70,00,000. Liabilities: business loan Rs. 50,00,000. Life insurance: term plan Rs. 2,00,00,000 (Rs. 2 crore). Financial goals: (1) Retire at age 60, maintain current lifestyle of Rs. 1,50,000 per month (in today's terms). (2) Daughter Priya's marriage in 3 years — current estimated cost Rs. 30,00,000 with general inflation of 8% p.a. on marriage expenses. (3) Smooth transfer of business to son Arjun. (4) Estate plan for family wealth distribution. Assumptions: General inflation 6% p.a., equity return 12% p.a., debt return 8% p.a., blended retirement return 9% p.a. Investment return for HLV calculation: 10% p.a. Question 5 of 5: Which tax-efficient strategy is most appropriate for Mahesh to transfer wealth to his children during his lifetime?

answer.text: Gift Rs. 5 crore directly to each child — gifts from parents are fully tax-free regardless of amount

Combination approach — gift financial assets to specified relatives (which are not chargeable under the gift provision), settle a family/private trust for business assets to enable sustainable inter-generational transfer, and use an existing HUF (if any) for additional tax efficiency on investment income
Create a new HUF and transfer all personal assets into it for tax-free partition later
Sell all assets, pay capital gains tax, and distribute the after-tax proceeds equally to both children

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook supports three building blocks for Mahesh's wealth-transfer plan: (1) Gifts to specified relatives (which include children) are not chargeable under the gift provision, so financial assets can be transferred to Arjun and Priya without triggering tax in their hands. (2) Clubbing provisions under Sections 60-64 apply in specified cases such as transfers to a minor child or spouse — since Arjun (25) and Priya (22) are adult children, clubbing does not apply to gifts made to them. (3) Family/private trusts are recognised vehicles for sustainable inter-generational transfer of business and other assets, allowing controlled distribution while preserving operational continuity. A combination approach therefore lets Mahesh transfer financial assets directly, ring-fence the business in a trust structure, and use any existing HUF for incremental tax efficiency on investment income. The Trap: Gifting Rs. 5 crore each in one stroke surrenders control immediately and may also trigger capital gains on non-cash assets at the donor's level before the gift. The new-HUF route is not a planning lever here — an HUF arises by operation of Hindu law and cannot simply be created at will to absorb personal assets. Selling all assets and distributing the proceeds triggers avoidable capital gains tax and defeats the inter-generational transfer objective. Note: Specified-relative gift relief, clubbing under Sections 60-64, and trust-based estate planning are covered across the NISM X-B workbook pages on gift taxation, clubbing of income, and trust structures.
